usage: leafy chives are counted in 단 (bundles)
a classic 전, especially popular on rainy days
raw chives lightly dressed; a common 반찬 with 삼겹살
송송 썰다 = to slice into small pieces
examples: Seasoned garlic chives go well with pork belly.
BBQ side; 어울리다 = to go well with
On rainy days I crave a garlic-chive pancake.
common saying; 생각나다 = to come to mind
One bunch of garlic chives is 2,000 won.
nuance: 부추 (garlic chives) are the flat, garlicky-smelling greens used for 부추전, 부추무침, and as a 만두 filling — not the same as thin 쪽파 (scallion). Regional note: the exact same vegetable is called 정구지 in much of 경상/전라, so you may hear that at markets. It's sold by the 단 and bruises easily, so use it fresh.
mistakes: Confusing 부추 (garlic chives) with 쪽파 (thin scallion)
Counting it with 개 instead of 단

usage: one bag of mung bean sprouts
sold by the bag at marts; 봉지 is the counter
blanched and tossed; a classic 반찬, also written 숙주 무침
a quick boil so they stay crunchy
tossed into 쌀국수, 잡채, and 만두소
examples: Mung bean sprouts go soft fast, so eat them quickly.
storage tip; 무르다 = to go soft
Please add lots of mung bean sprouts to the pho.
You should blanch mung bean sprouts only briefly so they stay crisp.
nuance: 숙주 (mung bean sprouts, full name 숙주나물) are the thinner, headless white sprouts — different from 콩나물, which have the yellow soybean head. At the store the two sit side by side, so check the label. 숙주 spoils fast and turns mushy within a day or two, so buy it the day you'll cook 쌀국수, 잡채, or 만두.
mistakes: Mixing up 숙주 (mung bean) with 콩나물 (soybean, has the yellow head)
Over-blanching it until it goes limp instead of staying crisp

usage: leafy greens are counted in 단 (bundles)
blanched and tossed with sesame oil and garlic
quick boil then rinse in cold water
무치다 = to dress with seasonings by hand
examples: You should only blanch spinach briefly so the color stays nice.
Today's side dish is seasoned spinach.
nuance: 시금치 is sold in bunches (단) and is a default ingredient for 나물 side dishes and for 잡채. Winter 시금치 (especially 섬초/포항초 varieties) is sweeter and prized. The verb pair to learn here is 데치다 (blanch) then 무치다 (season), which applies to most Korean leafy greens.
mistakes: Over-boiling it so it turns dark and mushy
Counting it with 개 instead of 단

usage: counted with 개; sold individually, often shrink-wrapped
채 썰다 = to cut into thin strips
sliced rounds in egg batter; a common 전
examples: I'll put zucchini in the soybean-paste stew.
I sliced the zucchini into rounds and made fritters.
nuance: 애호박 is the short, pale-green Korean zucchini — softer and sweeter than the dark Western 주키니/돼지호박. It's a staple in 된장찌개, 애호박전, and 호박나물. Residents should know 애호박 specifically, since just saying 호박 can mean pumpkin/squash more broadly.
mistakes: Using plain 호박 (which leans toward pumpkin) when you mean 애호박
Confusing it with cucumber (오이) because of the similar shape

usage: 표고 is the most common cooking mushroom
thin white clusters; great in 전골/hot pot
sold in packs (팩) at the mart
examples: Enoki mushrooms are delicious in hot pot.
Shiitake mushrooms have a strong aroma.
nuance: 버섯 is the general word; in practice you'll buy specific kinds — 표고 (shiitake), 팽이 (enoki), 새송이 (king oyster), 느타리 (oyster). They're cheap, sold in 팩, and central to 전골, 샤브샤브, and 불고기. Knowing at least 표고 and 팽이 by name covers most recipes and menus.
mistakes: Assuming 버섯 alone tells the seller which type you want
Pronouncing the final ㅅ as a clear 's' instead of an unreleased stop

usage: sold in bags; counter is 봉지 or by 장 for single leaves
marinated leaves eaten as a 반찬
wrap (meat) in perilla leaves and eat
쌈 culture; 싸 먹다 = to wrap and eat
distinctive minty-herbal smell some foreigners need to get used to
examples: 고기를 깻잎에 싸 먹으면 더 맛있어요.
Meat tastes better wrapped in perilla leaves.
Pickled perilla is the best side dish with rice.
깻잎 향이 처음엔 좀 강할 수 있어요.
The perilla smell can be a bit strong at first.
nuance: 깻잎 (perilla leaf) is NOT the same as 깨 (sesame seed) despite the name — it's the broad green leaf used for 쌈 and 장아찌. The pronunciation is roughly [깬닙], with the ㅅ+ㅇ creating an added ㄴ sound. Its strong herbal aroma is polarizing, so it's a real 'do you like it?' food among residents.
mistakes: Confusing 깻잎 (the leaf) with 깨 (sesame seeds)
Mispronouncing it; the linked sound is closer to [깬닙] than [깯입]

usage: leaf lettuce sold by the bag
쌈 = a wrap; the headline use of 상추
the go-to refill request at a BBQ place
you rinse leaf by leaf before wrapping
examples: Boss, can we get some more lettuce?
상추에 고기랑 마늘 올려서 싸 먹어요.
Put meat and garlic on the lettuce and wrap it to eat.
The lettuce is fresh, so it's crisp.
nuance: 상추 is the soft leaf lettuce used for 쌈 at Korean BBQ — distinct from 양상추 (iceberg/head lettuce) used in salads. '상추 좀 더 주세요' is one of the most useful restaurant phrases you'll ever learn, since refills are free. It's cheap, sold by the bag, and a fridge regular for anyone who grills meat at home.
mistakes: Mixing up 상추 (leaf lettuce) with 양상추 (iceberg lettuce)
Forgetting refills are free and not asking with '더 주세요'

usage: the big white radish, counted with 개
made from 무; a common kimchi type
examples: 국 끓일 때 무 넣으면 시원해요.
Adding radish when you make soup gives it a clean taste.
반 개 = half a one; useful since a whole 무 is big
Kkakdugi is kimchi made from radish.
nuance: 무 is the fat white Korean radish (daikon), milder and juicier than the Western red radish. It's the base of 무국, 깍두기, 동치미, and 무생채, and a whole one is large — so '반 개' (half) is a normal amount to buy. Note 시원하다 for radish soup means a clean, refreshing broth, not temperature.
mistakes: Picturing the small red Western radish instead of the large white 무
Thinking 시원한 국 means a cold soup rather than a clean-tasting one

usage: the base broth for many soups and 국수
big ones for stock vs small ones for 볶음
the classic base combo with 다시마
examples: Stir-fried anchovies often come as a standing side dish.
For broth anchovies, you remove the guts before using.
real prep step; 똥 here = the dark gut
nuance: 멸치 (dried anchovy) comes in sizes by purpose: big 국물용 for broth, small 볶음용 for the stir-fried 반찬. With 다시마 (kelp) it forms the default Korean soup stock. A practical tip residents learn: pull out the dark gut from large anchovies so the broth isn't bitter.
mistakes: Using tiny snack anchovies for broth instead of the large 국물용
Boiling them too long, which makes the stock bitter

usage: meat is often sold by the 근, which is 600 g (not 500)
the most popular cut for grilling
cheaper cut, good for 제육볶음 and stews
examples: Give me one geun of pork, please.
I'm going to make spicy stir-fried pork for dinner.
For soup meat, beef is better than pork.
comparing cuts; 국거리 = meat for soup
nuance: 돼지고기 (pork) is the everyday meat in Korea, cheaper than 소고기 (beef) and central to 삼겹살, 제육볶음, and 김치찌개. The key practical point is the unit: at a butcher or mart, meat is sold by the 근, and for meat one 근 = 600 g, so '한 근' is more than a pound. Learn the cut names — 삼겹살 (belly), 목살 (neck/collar), 앞다리살 (shoulder).
mistakes: Assuming a 근 of meat is 500 g — for meat it's 600 g
Saying just 고기 when the butcher needs to know 돼지고기 vs 소고기

usage: a full 판 is 30 eggs; the standard bulk unit at marts
single eggs are counted with 알
spoken 계란후라이 is more common, but 프라이 is the standard spelling
풀다 here = to whisk/loosen eggs before cooking
examples: How much is a tray of eggs?
Beat an egg into your ramen and eat it.
everyday tip; 풀다 = to whisk in
I made and ate a fried egg this morning.
casual; 해 먹다 = to cook for oneself
nuance: 계란 is the everyday word for egg and what you'll see on most cartons and menus; 달걀 is the slightly more 'proper'/textbook word for the same thing, so both are correct. Eggs are sold by the 판 (a tray of 30) for bulk or by smaller packs, and a single egg is counted with 알. Note 노른자 (yolk) and 흰자 (white) are worth knowing for recipes.
mistakes: Counting eggs with 개 instead of 알 (or buying by the 판)
Assuming 계란 and 달걀 are different things — they're the same egg, just different register

usage: common amount, since a whole one is big
steamed cabbage leaves for wrapping with 쌈장
examples: I want to buy just half a head of cabbage.
I steam the cabbage and eat it as wraps.
Pork cutlet comes with shredded cabbage.
nuance: 양배추 is the round Western-style head cabbage — keep it separate from 배추 (the long napa cabbage used for kimchi). It's counted with 통 (whole) and commonly bought as 반 통 since a full head is large. Shredded 양배추 is the standard side with 돈가스, and steamed leaves make a mild 쌈.
mistakes: Mixing up 양배추 (round cabbage) with 배추 (napa cabbage for kimchi)
Counting it with 개 instead of 통
